intro_html: San bei ji, three cup chicken, is named for the three liquids that make it: sesame oil, soy sauce, and rice wine, traditionally a cup of each. Chicken braises in that mixture with a startling amount of garlic and ginger until the sauce reduces to a syrup, and then a mountain of fresh basil goes in at the very end. Each bowl runs 689 calories and 54 grams of protein for about $4.58 a serving (at everyday cost).
cost_closing_html: About $4.58 a bowl (at everyday cost). The basil is the expensive line, which feels backwards until you taste the dish, because basil is not a garnish here. It is one of the main ingredients.
shop_smart: Fresh basil is the biggest cost in this recipe by a wide margin. If you have any growing space at all, a basil plant on a windowsill pays for itself in about two batches of this dish and keeps producing all summer.
Boneless thighs are the correct cut and the cheap one. Three cup chicken reduces hard, and breast meat would be sawdust by the time the sauce is right.

Toasted sesame oil is not the same product as plain sesame oil, and it is used in real volume here rather than as a finishing drizzle. Buy the bigger bottle, since it is the flavor backbone of the dish.
Garlic by the bag is dramatically cheaper than the pre-peeled tubs, and this recipe uses a serious amount of it. Whole heads also keep for weeks on the counter.
make_it: Weigh your empty mixing pot and write the number down for portioning later.
Cut the chicken thighs into large bite sized pieces and pat them very dry.

Heat the sesame oil and vegetable oil together in a wide pan over medium heat and fry the sliced ginger until the edges curl and go slightly crisp. Do not rush this, because that fried ginger is a signature of the dish.
Add the whole peeled garlic cloves and the dried arbol chiles and cook until the garlic turns golden. Whole cloves, not minced. They go sweet and soft during the braise.
Turn the heat up, add the chicken, and brown it on all sides.

Pour in the soy sauce, chicken broth, and sugar, bring it to a boil, then simmer uncovered 20 to 25 minutes while the sauce reduces down and turns glossy and dark. Stir now and then so nothing catches.
Kill the heat, throw in the entire pile of basil leaves, and stir just until they wilt. Ten seconds. Basil cooked any longer than that turns black and loses everything.
portion_html: Weigh the rice into each container first, then put the pan on the scale, subtract the empty weight you wrote down, and divide by 14. Get sauce into every container, since it is concentrated and a little goes a long way. Each portion lands at 689 calories.

head.description: Taiwanese three cup chicken with sesame oil, soy sauce, whole garlic, and fresh basil over rice, rebuilt for 14 meal prep servings at about $4.58 a bowl (at everyday cost).

steps: Cut and dry the chicken thighs and start the rice.
Fry sliced ginger in sesame and vegetable oil until the edges curl.
Add whole garlic cloves and dried chiles and cook until golden.
Brown the chicken, then add soy sauce, broth, and sugar.
Simmer uncovered 20 to 25 minutes until the sauce reduces and glazes.
Kill the heat, stir in the basil until just wilted, and portion with rice into 14 containers.
